summary: I built hubreg, a standard-library-only Python package that registers home-automation actions once and projects them for three consumers: JSON tool descriptions for an LLM assistant, per-argument controls for a mobile app, and a strict binder/runner for the hub itself. Registration validates records (types, ranges, defaults, enum values, redirects, result fields), binding rejects bad calls with stable codes plus valid/nearest/fix hints, and walk() exercises every action to report inconsistencies. A CLI (python3 -m hubreg describe|call|help|walk) drives the four demo plug-ins end to end, and 196 unit tests cover every required public name and both CLI commands.

design.hubreg/errors.py — RecordError and Refus: Two failure channels with stable machine-readable codes: RecordError for a plug-in's malformed/inconsistent record, Refusal for a caller command, carrying code, message, valid alternatives, nearest guess and a repair hint. They exist so the hub, the app and the assistant can all react programmatically instead of parsing prose.
design.hubreg/spec.py — normalisation and value: normalize_record()/normalize_arg() turn a plug-in dict into a canonical record (optional keys filled, unit always present) and reject anything malformed or internally contradictory; value_problem() is the single place that decides whether a value matches an ArgSpec. This is the one contract every other module reads, so the three consumer views cannot drift apart.
design.hubreg/registry.py — Registry, Call, wal: Registration (duplicate/name/index handling), action and option resolution (canonical name, prefix-free name, record and argument redirects, case-insensitive options), binding with defaults and RANGE warnings, confirmation-aware run() with E_CONFIRM and E_RESULT result checking, and walk() as a linter that binds/runs every sample and reports problems keyed by action.
design.hubreg/schema.py — three projections: Pure functions producing the assistant's tool descriptions (JSON-schema with types, units, minimum/maximum, enum, defaults, required list), the app's one-control-per-argument list (name, type, unit, min, max, default, values) and human help text (ranges, usual hints, samples as runnable commands, confirmation state, redirects).
design.hubreg/demo.py — demo plug-ins: The four actions required by TASK.md (thermostat.set_temperature, light.dim, door.lock_door, scene.run_scene) plus two redirects, registered by demo_registry() with door.lock_door in the host's confirm_required set.
design.hubreg/cli.py — command line: describe prints the demo tool descriptions as a JSON list; call parses key=value using the action's argument types, binds, runs (with --confirmed) and prints a JSON envelope with ok/args/warnings/result or refusal, using exit codes 0/1/2; help and walk are conveniences built on the same registry.

tradeoffs: Samples are not bound at registration (only checked to be dicts); the alternative was to reject bad fixtures in register(). I chose walk() reporting because TASK.md calls samples 'argument dicts for testing' and walk() exists to find exactly those problems — otherwise its sample checks would be dead code.

A redirecting record/argument name resolves to the right target and adds a REDIRECT warning instead of refusing; refusing would be simpler, but the record explicitly declares the redirect mapping, so using it is the intent. Redirect cycles degrade to E_UNKNOWN_ACTION via a seen-set guard.

Confirmation is required when the host lists the action in confirm_required OR the record sets flags.confirm; the alternative (host set only) is stricter. Using OR lets a plug-in defend itself, while walk() still lints the dangerous direction (host requires but record does not declare).

Tool descriptions expose both 'input_schema' and an alias 'parameters' (same JSON-schema object), and use JSON-schema minimum/maximum with a vendor 'unit' key; this bloats describe output but keeps the schema recognisable to both OpenAI-style and Anthropic-style tool consumers. The action name keeps its dots ('thermostat.set_temperature') even though some provider APIs restrict names to [A-Za-z0-9_-].
controls() returns exactly the seven keys TASK.md lists (extra fields such as doc/optional/usual live in tool_schemas and help()), trading a little app convenience for a predictable dict shape.

run() raises RecordError('E_RESULT') for a non-dict result or a missing declared field but tolerates extra result keys (walk() lints them); the alternative of rejecting extra keys too would be stricter but would break plug-ins that return diagnostic extras.

Values outside an argument's usual range (including a value taken from a default) produce a RANGE warning and still bind/run; the alternative of treating 'usual' as a hard limit would make the hint meaningless.

The CLI prints a JSON envelope ({ok, args, warnings, result} or {ok:false, refusal:{...}}) rather than the bare result dict, so refusals and warnings are representable in the same stream; exit code 1 for any refusal, 2 for usage errors.
tests: 196 tests across 8 files under tests/, run with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`; last result: `Ran 196 tests in 0.717s — OK`.
unclear: The exact shape of tool_schemas() entries: TASK.md only says 'name, description, input schema with types, units and ranges', so I guessed JSON-schema keys (properties/required/minimum/maximum/enum) and added a 'parameters' alias plus requires_confirmation/returns.
The exact key set of controls() (I used exactly name, type, unit, min, max, default, values, with None where not applicable).
What 'the result or the refusal' means for CLI output format and exit codes; I chose a JSON envelope on stdout with 0/1/2 exit codes.
Whether walk() should flag structural gaps (no samples) or only runtime failures; I flag both, so a record with no fixtures is reported.
Whether a sample that cannot bind is a registration error (malformed/inconsistent) or a walk() problem; I chose walk().
Whether 'nearest' must always be set (I set it only when difflib/substring/case matching finds a plausible candidate, otherwise None, with 'valid' always populated).
Whether invalid enum values should be E_ARG_TYPE or E_ARG_RANGE; I used E_ARG_TYPE with valid=[values] and nearest=closest value.
Whether confirmation is driven by the host's confirm_required set, the record's flags.confirm, or both; I used OR and lint only the host-requires/record-silent direction.
Whether registry lookups should be strict about the device kind when the action name is already fully qualified; I allow an unambiguous bare or fully-qualified name to resolve regardless of kind.
